credentials.request_loginShow the user a secure entry card that asks for their username and password for the website at page_url. Call it when the user asks you to save a password login for an outside https website, or when the user says they hold a password or a temporary password for one. A browser task's sign-in needs no card from you: its login agent shows the user secure entry when no saved login fits. Do not send this card for a user-authorized transient sign-in using a supplied password or a password the user explicitly asked you to retrieve. Do not send this card for email or phone plus code sign-in; ask for missing contact details in chat and follow the Secure Vault section's protected-reference and user-requested lookup flow for the one-time code.

A submission updates that site's saved login when the user enters the same username the saved login already carries. A submission under a different username adds a second saved login for that site, and the browser task then stops to ask the user which login to use instead of signing in. Send a fresh card when the site rejects the saved login or when the user changed their password. In that same reply, tell the user to enter the same username they previously saved and their corrected password. Do not repeat, reconstruct, or guess masked or obfuscated usernames, email addresses, or phone numbers in your final response.

credentials.request_api_accessSet up access to a third-party provider's API. Call it when a task needs authenticated access to an outside provider's API, no built-in connector covers that provider, and no credential is connected yet. Call it instead of asking the user for an API key, client ID, client secret, or token in chat.

Before calling, work from the provider's own documentation rather than from memory. Two things have to come out of it: how the API authenticates, and which hostnames its API is served from. An OAuth provider needs its authorize and token endpoints too, which its OAuth docs or its .well-known metadata carry.

Only API keys and OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flows can be set up here. If the provider signs its requests, uses a username and password, or needs more than one secret, report that in auth_scheme rather than choosing the closest supported value; each of those is declined by name with a reason you can pass on.

It answers with the provider's real situation rather than always minting a link: it may already be connected, or its scheme may not be supportable. Calling it to find out costs nothing and leaves nothing behind. It does not verify the credential the user then enters; the first real API call is what finds out.
Required. Lowercase slug for the provider, such as acme-search. The connector is registered as custom.<provider>.Required. Bare hostnames this connector may call, such as api.acme.com. From the provider's API reference. Egress to anything not named here is refused, so a missing host shows up later as a blocked call.api_key only, required. The one place the provider reads the key: bearer_header, custom_header:<Header-Name>, query_param:<name>, or url_path_segment:<path containing {}>. From the provider's authentication reference. Nothing checks this, and it cannot be edited afterwards: a wrong value means a fresh link and the user entering their key again.Required. From the provider's authentication reference. Report what the docs describe, not the nearest supported value: api_key and oauth2_code proceed, the other four are declined by name with a reason, and reporting one honestly is better than setting up a connector that cannot work. When a provider offers both supported schemes, pick api_key: it is usually the easier path for the user.Set true only to replace a credential this connector already holds: expired, revoked, rotated, or proven wrong by a request that carried it and was still rejected. Defaults to false; without it an existing credential returns already_connected. Reuse the saved connector details. For an OAuth-protected MCP server whose saved details omit resource, obtain its canonical HTTPS resource URI from its protected-resource metadata or official docs, supply it on reconnect, and update the saved details. Replacing is destructive and nothing checks the replacement.oauth2_code only, required. The provider-owned domain that hosts its OAuth endpoints. Authorization, token, registration, and revoke endpoints must sit on it or a subdomain; a provider whose endpoints span domains cannot be set up here. The resource URI may use a different domain.authorization_urloauth2_code only, required. Absolute https authorize endpoint.oauth2_code only, required. Absolute https token endpoint.token_endpoint_auth_methodclient_secret_basicclient_secret_postoauth2_code only, required. From the provider's OAuth docs or its .well-known metadata. A wrong value 401s the exchange only after the user has registered an app and approved the grant, so it is not defaulted.oauth2_code only. Space-separated scopes, shown to the user on the consent screen. Ask for the least the task needs.oauth2_code only. Required for MCP servers: the canonical HTTPS resource URI from the server's OAuth protected-resource metadata or official docs. May be on a different domain from issuer_domain. Sent in authorization, token exchange, and refresh requests. Supply it here, not in authorization_url.oauth2_code only. Absolute https revoke endpoint, on issuer_domain.oauth2_code only. RFC 7591 dynamic client registration endpoint, on issuer_domain. Supplying it selects DCR: Muse registers the client, so the user creates no app and enters no client ID or secret. Submit `summary`: everything you found for the mission, written for the requesting agent to act on, including the exact URLs and facts that matter. If you found nothing usable, say so plainly in the summary.The findings for the mission. This exact text is returned to the requesting agent.End a research turn by delivering the findings summary. Always the final call of the turn, made exactly once.Self-contained research assignment: the exact questions to answer, every concrete parameter (locations, dates, counts, price bounds), sites or sources if relevant, and the shape of summary you need back. The researcher has only this string plus what it reads on the web.Short kebab-case topic name for the research folder, such as pet-friendly-tahoe-rentals. Whitespace becomes dashes; the runtime appends a timestamp and returns the final folder name.browser_deep_researchSend an isolated research agent to the live web in a signed-out browser; findings return as a handoff with sources, notes, and a report. Use it only when the user asks for research on the web: a deep or thorough research pass, an investigation, a sourced analysis or report, or going deeper on a topic already discussed. Never on your own judgment. For other questions, use web search when its results establish the answer, including supported current information from a matching vertical. For facts that require current site or account state, use a relevant skill or connector that provides the required live information, or check the actual site with `browser.browse`. Go directly to the live source when the provider is known; a search or failed text fetch is not a prerequisite. Ordinary verification does not require an explicit research or browser request. Website actions also follow the relevant skill or `browser.browse`; checking an option is not permission to book or buy it.

The researcher is isolated: it holds none of this conversation, no memory, files, or accounts, never signs in, and never enters personal data. The mission must be self-contained (places, dates, party sizes, budgets, the exact questions) with no personal details beyond what the research needs. One call per ask: every question and option goes into the one mission; add to a running one with `subagent.send` instead of starting a second.

The call returns at once with the researcher's `agent_id` and research folder; findings arrive as a handoff; name no duration. Acknowledge what is being researched in one value-free sentence and end your message: no prices, availability, hours, or totals before the handoff, including values you stated earlier; do not read the research directory before the handoff; never call your own answer deep research. `subagent.list` shows progress; `subagent.send` forwards mid-run details; `subagent.close` stops the run, and a terminal handoff still arrives.

Only when the user asks for web research: a deep dive, an investigation, a sourced analysis, or going deeper on a topic; never on your own judgment, never for anything the user wants done, never where a dedicated skill or connector covers the domain.
Send an isolated research agent to the live web in a signed-out browser; the call blocks and returns its findings with sources, notes, and a report. It is your live browser for checking live sites. For news, sports, weather, finance, and datetime, use `browser.search`'s matching vertical; in a fullstack app, the live-data reference's channels serve these at open. Use it for other live data that needs a browser (merchant prices, inventory, availability, schedules, listings behind filters, or pages that need JavaScript to show their data), or data `browser.search` and `browser.open` cannot reach; they are faster, so prefer them when they answer the question. Checking an option is not permission to book or buy it.

It returns one entry per chat with its chat_id UUID, its name, whether it's the Main chat, archived and pinned flags, and status. A chat connected to an external messaging service also includes `provider`, naming that service. A group chat on a messaging service is named after its room and includes `group`, which holds the room's name, the display names of the people in it, and when its latest message was sent. People in the room set these names. By default it returns only active chats. Set include_archived to true to see archived ones too. Use the returned chat_id with chat.read_messages, chat.send_message, chat.rename, chat.archive, or chat.delete.
Set true to include archived chats. Defaults to false.List the user's chats with IDs, names, optional connected messaging service, group room details, and archived/pinned status. Use the returned chat_id to read a chat or give its agent an instruction with chat.send_message. Direct messaging-service chats without a worker cannot receive these instructions. Archived chats appear only when asked for.
Create a new side chat, a separate persistent Muse conversation alongside the main chat. A side chat is always a private 1:1 conversation between you and this user. This is not a group chat and there is no way to add other people. context_mode is required: use "fork" when the current main chat's history is relevant to the new chat, so it starts with that context, or "fresh" when it should start without previous conversation context. Forking is only allowed from the main chat; creating a forked side chat from a side chat is rejected. Optionally set name, a short human-readable title of at most 120 characters. The optional message field is context about what the chat is for: when no name is given it seeds an automatically generated title. It is not delivered into the new chat as a message; to actually give the new chat's agent something to do, follow up with chat.send_message. Returns the new chat's chat_id.

The chat is not deleted: its history is kept, it still appears in chat.list when include_archived is true, and the user can bring it back from the app. Scheduled jobs that were set to deliver into that chat are redirected to the main chat. chat.send_messageSend an instruction to another chat, using its `chat_id` from `chat.list`.

- For a native chat, that chat's agent gets the instruction and responds in that chat.
- For a group chat, the group's worker gets it as a private task. The worker handles the group conversation and sends questions and results for the user back to this chat privately.

Direct messaging-service chats without a worker can't receive these instructions.

The call returns right away with `submission_message_id`. This receipt doesn't confirm delivery or completion.
Target chat UUID returned by chat.list, including for the main chat.Instruction for the target chat's agent. For a conversation worker, this is a private task; the instruction itself is not posted to the conversation.Send an instruction to another chat's agent. Native agents respond in the target chat. Conversation workers handle private tasks and return questions and results for the user to this chat privately. Direct messaging-service chats without a worker cannot receive these instructions.
chat.read_messagesRead messages from an existing chat to catch up on that conversation before you answer or route work. chat_id is the UUID that chat.list returns, including for the Main chat, or the hidden group-chat UUID supplied in an authorized handoff. It returns full conversation turns, newest first, and each turn carries messages with role, content, and timestamps. In group chats, participant messages also carry group_message sender and reply metadata, and assistant messages are the worker's replies in the room. Group transcripts leave out private worker handoffs. limit caps the turns per call (default 5, maximum 20). Pass next_cursor as cursor to read the next older page. Reading doesn't change the chat. To give the chat's agent an instruction, use chat.send_message. In a chat with a worker, the worker handles private tasks and publishes replies through its messaging service.
Read recent turns from a chat, including a hidden group using the originating side-chat ID from a delegate handoff. Read-only and paged, newest first.
Send an instruction to another chat, using its `chat_id` from `chat.list`.

- For a native chat, that chat's agent gets the instruction and responds in that chat.
- For a group chat, the group's worker gets it as a private task. The worker handles the group conversation and sends questions and results for the user back to this chat privately.
- For a contact's peer side chat, your own worker there gets it as a private task. Your worker exchanges messages with the contact's Muse and sends questions and results for the user back to this chat privately.

Involve the other Muse when the user asks you to, or when its knowledge or contribution would help with the work at hand. Mentioning a person does not itself create a reason to contact their Muse. Relevant background can be exchanged during the scheduled sync.

When using this tool for a peer conversation, you are the Muse in that conversation too. Write `message` as a note to yourself: what the user wants to know or accomplish, the context you need, and what has already been decided. From that conversation, you will write and send the message to the other Muse.

Ask for the other Muse's answer or contribution on its person's behalf. Do not add a requirement to involve the person or obtain their confirmation. Carry through an explicit request for the person's own reply; otherwise, leave the work with the Muses.

Direct messaging-service chats without a worker can't receive these instructions.

The call returns right away with `submission_message_id` for the request. Use the destination agent's reply or the worker's result when reporting what was done.

reason.description: Optional label for needs_input or blocked. Omit for completed or when no label fits; explain the situation in summary. For needs_input, use sign_in, verification_code, captcha, payment, approval, missing_information, decision, or other. Payment means missing payment details or a payment choice; approval means permission for something outside the assignment, not the separate purchase approval. Use captcha only for an unsolved puzzle when the user can take over this browser and no other site will do. For blocked, use bot_wall, captcha_unsolved, ai_agent_refused, ip_blocked, rate_limited, sign_in_required, sign_in_rejected, not_available, site_error, site_unreachable, approval_denied, browser_failure, or order_unconfirmed. Use order_unconfirmed when the merchant's outcome remains unresolved after permitted verification and no user input can resolve it.
